setting.genre: grounded low fantasy, survival and settlement
setting.tone: grounded and warm near camp, stranger and more hostile deeper in
setting.era: pre-industrial frontier: flint and bronze in the valley, iron and river trade downriver
setting.description:
Aederyn is a river valley, ringed by hills, that has been closed to the outside world for about 120 years. Nobody downriver remembers why. The Crown's maps mark it as impassable, and the old roads into it end at a line of standing stones and a wall of weather that nobody could get through. This spring the weather broke. A charter company got a licence from the Crown to settle the valley, and its boats tied up at the valley mouth. The player is one of the first settlers.

The valley looks empty and fertile. The camp at the southern mouth sits in open meadow with a stream, gorse scrub and the stones of old field walls in the grass. The walls are the first clue that people lived here once. North of camp the Southwood's birch and oak close in. The Scarp's hills and an old mine rise on the west flank, and the Sinks' fens and lake spread across the east. Past both lies the Wardline, a band of walled farmland gone wild with a ring of wardstones standing in it. Inside the ring is the Bloom, a forest smothered in pale fungal growth. At its centre is the Heart, where the growth comes up out of the ground.

What the settlers don't know is that the valley was sealed on purpose. About 120 years ago a fungus began to spread through the ground under the valley. It is a single vast network that takes hosts, animals and then people, and grows through them. The valley's Wardens raised a ward to hold it in, a ring of inscribed stones drawing on the bedrock. They didn't tell everyone. The families in the upper valley were sealed inside with it. Some adapted and survived as the descendants, a wary, closed community with a holdfast in the Wardline. Others gave themselves to the network to live. Their bodies became hosts, husks that stand still in the growth until something disturbs them. Their children, born inside the network, are the hybrids, people who think and feel, are strange, and are at peace with the fungus.

The ward has weakened, and that is why the weather broke. The fungus is not evil. It is an ecology spreading the way ecologies do, and deeper in the valley everything is more overgrown, more colonised and more dangerous. Spores drain health and have to be filtered. Colonised animals fight differently from the ones near camp. Better gear comes from further in, so going somewhere new is how a player grows stronger.

Four groups want different things. The charter company wants a profitable settlement and knows nothing about the ward. The Wardens, down to a few old members, want the ward repaired and have kept quiet about what they did, because the truth is damning. The descendants want a reckoning from the Wardens more than anything else. The hybrids want the ward broken, because they see the fungus as the valley's next step and the ward as a cage. There's no clean answer. Mending the ward protects the settlement and condemns a thinking people. Breaking it frees them and lets the fungus spread.

For players this is a story told by pushing inward: at first about gathering, crafting and making camp, and then, region by region, about the people who were here first and what was done to them.

themes.name: Frontier and Home
themes.description: The camp is the seed of a settlement, and the early game is about making a place liveable: tools, food, shelter, a fire that's always lit. Camp stays warm and safe, and every trip out ends with a trip back. The valley is a frontier to the settlers, but it was somebody's home, and the traces of it (field walls, a forged hinge, a name on a stone) turn up in the ordinary work of settling.
examples: Camp's rest heals faster than anywhere else, so every expedition starts and ends there
Old field walls and a forged iron hinge in the Landing are the first signs of earlier people
The contract board's ordinary jobs keep sending players back to regions they've outgrown
Camp's cast are tradespeople with plain ambitions: a workshop, a kitchen with walls, a share of land

themes.name: What Was Sealed In
themes.description: The ward kept something in, and also kept people in who were never asked. The truth comes out slowly, through what players find and what the Wardens are finally made to confess. It's damning without being a simple villain story: the Wardens made a terrible choice under real pressure, and are still living with it.
examples: Ansel Morrow's confession questline, told in pieces as players prove themselves
Descendant family names that match old Warden records
Sister Edith's journals and inscriptions at the Seventh Stone
The descendants' demand for a reckoning, which stands apart from the question of the ward

themes.name: Growth, Not Evil
themes.description: The fungus is an ecology, not a malice. It takes hosts because that is how it grows. Deeper in, the valley becomes stranger and more hostile without ever becoming a dark lord's domain. The hybrids make that case in person: they think, feel and choose, and they see the ward as a cage around the valley's next step. Players are left to weigh a thinking people against a settlement's safety.
examples: Spore strength rises by tier, from the Wardline to the Bloom to the Heart
Colonised animals are ordinary creatures, changed: a heron, a mossback wolf, an elk
Hosts stand still until disturbed; they don't hunt
Sporecraft is stronger than warding but leaves its user always slightly exposed
The repair-or-break choice at the Heart has no clean answer

systems.name: Effects and Spores
systems.description: Places, gear and consumables put ongoing effects on a player: spores that drain health, cold water that slows gathering, dark that blocks work without a light, rest that heals, and bountiful ground that speeds gathering. Negative effects rise with depth, and gear softens them but never cancels them outright, so every expedition has a clock on it and ends back at camp or with a tincture. Spores are the valley's signature hazard. They thicken tier by tier toward the Heart, and filtering them is what makes the Wardline and beyond survivable. In the Wardline they drain about 1 health every 5 seconds; the Sinks' moss spore-wrap cuts that by about a third, the holdfast's waxed mask by half, and a spore tincture on top of the mask to about a third, never to nothing. The holdfast's mugwort smudge fires filter the air inside its walls, so it's somewhere to rest.
rules: Spores drain health over time and stop natural healing; masks, respirators and tinctures filter them
Cold (in the Sinks) slows gathering; waders and dry layers soften it
Dark (in the deep Scarp mine) blocks gathering and fighting until you carry a light
Rest at camp and the holdfast heals faster; bountiful ground speeds gathering
Effects from a place, worn gear and consumables add together
limitations: No gear makes a player immune to spores or cold: some always gets through
Consumable protection wears off and must be replaced
Lights take the off hand, competing with a shield

systems.name: Warding
systems.description: The craft of stone, order and containment that raised the ward. A warder cuts lines into wardstone with a stylus and draws on the valley's bedrock through them. A line holds a thing by knowing its shape, so a Warden's first work is to cut a shard closed around a piece of what it must hold. Bound to a yew staff with bronze and gut, the shard carries the line from the ground through the warder into whatever they strike: it doesn't cut, it holds and presses, so shells and hides that turn a blade are no help. Ansel Morrow teaches it at the warding table at camp's edge once a player has brought him wardstone from the Scarp and pale growth from the Sinks, and gives them his own stylus. A wardstone focus is the next step: a shard cut closed around a host's grey threads and set in Warden steel, which presses on hosts harder than any blade and can hold a cracked stone's lines for a while. The ward itself is the same craft at its largest: twelve wardstones cut from the Scarp seam, set in a ring across the middle of the valley, holding the network in. Lesser boundary stones marked the edge of what was moved out. The ring is failing: boundary stones are cracking from the outside, and the threads have begun to grow along the lines themselves.
rules: Warding draws on the valley's bedrock through lines cut in wardstone
A line holds a thing by knowing its shape: shards are cut around a piece of what they hold
It's taught by the Wardens at the warding table, and cutting a line needs a Warden's stylus
The ward itself is a ring of twelve wardstones around the upper valley
Its weapons are focus-staves and wardstone foci; they strike with magic, which stone, shell and a host's thick body don't turn
The ring was keyed from the Heart, where the first line was cut; every stone answers to it
limitations: It holds and contains: it can't heal what the fungus has taken
Every line must be closed and exact, so it's slow to learn and slow to make
A cracked line fails, and the network can grow along the grooves of one
The ring was raised at a cost the Wardens still won't speak of

systems.name: Sporecraft
systems.description: The hybrids' craft of growth and the network: coaxing the fungus to grow, burst and bind for the user. Where warding presses a thing into the shape of a line, sporecraft feeds a thing until it wants to spread and points it. Gill teaches it at the growing pit in the Bloom, and only to those Gill trusts, who are given a chitin dibber to open the beds. Things are grown there, not forged: the Sporecraft Wand from threaded heartwood, a host's threads, spore resin and chitin, and Thread Balm from resin, a mycelium mat and honey. It is stronger than warding, and it carries the network with it: the wand breathes spores on whoever holds it, anywhere in the valley, so a sporecrafter never heals on their own and is never entirely clean. The balm knits a wound faster than comfrey and leaves the Bloom in the chest for a while. Choosing between warding and sporecraft mirrors the choice between repairing the ward and breaking it.
rules: Taught by the hybrids at the growing pit in the Bloom, from tier 4, with a chitin dibber only Gill gives
Sporecraft weapons are grown, not forged, from fungal material
Every sporecraft weapon carries a worn spores effect on its user, in or out of the Bloom
It bursts rather than presses: it goes through what warding can't shape, and slides off the grown crust of hosts, elk and moths like warding does
limitations: The user is always slightly exposed to spores while carrying it: it stops natural healing everywhere, and only rest or a mask outpaces it
The hybrids teach it only to those who have earned their trust, which the Wardens won't forgive

systems.name: The Crafting Ladder
systems.description: Tools, weapons and armour are made from materials, and each tier's materials come from that tier's region. Players climb from flint, wood and linen in the Landing to bone and hide in the Southwood, bronze from the Scarp with strings, waders and glass from the Sinks, iron and salvaged Warden steel in the Wardline, chitin and mycelium leather in the Bloom, and in the Heart only what its guardians drop: heartshell, grown sinew, humming thread and a Warden's old respirator. Basic stations are at camp and specialist ones at regional landmarks, each with a face who runs it.
rules: Each region's materials make that tier's gear, and going somewhere new is how you upgrade
The Scarp and the Sinks are interdependent: tier 2 needs both
Iron sits in the deep Scarp behind the dark, a tier-3 material in a tier-2 region
The Heart has no gathering, only drops and rewards
limitations: Tools and weapons wear out and must be replaced or remade
Deeper materials need better tools to gather, and better gear to survive gathering them

factions.name: The Charter Company
factions.description: A trading company from downriver holding the Crown's charter to settle the valley. It paid for the boats, the tents and the stores, and it expects the settlement to pay that back. It runs the camp through a quartermaster and a contract board of paid jobs. It's practical, commercial and not cruel. It also knows nothing about the ward or the people behind it, and it thinks the valley is empty land. As players learn the truth, the company is the voice of the settlement's ordinary interest: safety, profit and the people who came to build a life.
goals: Turn the camp into a settlement that repays the charter
Survey and claim the valley's land and resources
Keep settlers working and safe enough to stay
members: Settlers working for a share of land

factions.name: The Wardens
factions.description: The order that kept the valley's bedrock craft and, about 120 years ago, raised the ward that sealed the fungus in, along with everyone who lived in the upper valley. They were sworn to silence about what the ward was for and who was on the wrong side of it. The order has dwindled to a few old members, and most people downriver have never heard of it. Its last Wardens come back to the valley as it reopens. They know what's out there, want the ward repaired, and keep quiet because the truth is damning. Their gradual confession, and the warding they teach, is a story spine. Ansel Morrow has admitted to players that the twelve stones hold a single living thing under the upper valley and that the ring is failing, and has handed his own stylus to one of them. Once they find the holdfast and read Sister Edith's journal at the Seventh Stone, he admits the rest of the order's part: the upper families were left on purpose, because the Keepers feared they'd carry the growth downriver, and they weren't told, because people who are told run. His master confessed it to him on his deathbed. His own part came out last. At nineteen he re-cut the Sixth Stone while a child held on to it from inside and called to him, and he finished the line. The Heart-Warden is Keeper Joss Wicken, who keyed the first line with his brother's family inside it. Ansel said all of it once, at Wick's gate, with Sister Edith's book in his hands, then went to the Sixth Stone and said it again to the child, who was Gill. He still asks for the ring to be re-cut, knowing what it costs, and says he shouldn't be the one to choose.
goals: Repair the ward before the fungus spreads beyond the valley
Keep what was done to the abandoned from coming out, for as long as they can
Pass on warding to someone who can finish the work
members: Warden-Keepers, the old masters of the craft, who decided who would be left
Sworn Wardens, bound to a wardstone and a square house beside it
Their journals, rolls and inscriptions, left at the stones

factions.name: The Descendants
factions.description: The children and grandchildren of the valley families who were sealed inside the ward without warning, and who adapted rather than turned. About seventy of them live in the holdfast, a walled farm hamlet in the middle of the Wardline, behind a gate of silvered oak and pans of smouldering mugwort. They keep sheep inside the wall, farm what fields they can hold, and live on what the Reed women's stillroom makes: felt masks packed with mugwort and waxed stiff, tinctures of mugwort and honey, comfrey salves. They're small, suspicious and proud. They don't go out to the hosts, whom they call walkers and still half think of as kin, and they resent the outside world that walled them in. Their names are settler names worn down over 120 years with a byname added, and the families match the Wardens' roll of the upper farms (Wicken, Reed, Dunning, Hale, Thackery). Old Wick, the elder, keeps the gate and the grudge; Tam Reedsdaughter, the young healer, keeps the stillroom and wants to see downriver. A player earns standing by helping the holdfast against the hounds and walkers; then the gate opens, and so do Tam's loom and apothecary and the holdfast's own contract board. They want a reckoning from the Wardens more than they want the ward mended or broken, and they get it: Ansel Morrow confesses the whole of it at the gate, Edith's book is carried to the holdfast and read to the children, and Wick learns that the Keeper still standing in the Heart is his grandmother's uncle. Having got it, Wick won't choose for the stones. If they're re-cut, Tam goes up to the Sixth Stone every dusk to talk to a cousin who can't come down; if they're opened, Gill walks through the gate, and the north ditch goes white overnight.
goals: A reckoning: a Warden saying out loud, in front of the holdfast, what the order did
Keep the holdfast safe, fed and independent of the company
Hold their ground between the settlers and the turned
members: Elders who heard it from those who were left, like Old Wick
Healers and mask-makers of the stillroom, like Tam Reedsdaughter

factions.name: The Hybrids
factions.description: Children of the turned, born inside the fungal network to parents who became its hosts. They think, feel and speak, though strangely, and they're at peace with the fungus in a way no outsider is. They call the hosts the parents and tend them, sweeping round their feet, and they hear what the parents remember through the threads: Gill learned Davy Reed's song from the ground before learning words. They live in the Bloom and teach sporecraft at its growing pit, and post their own work there (resin, mats, where the puffballs have burst). The ward holds the network, and them with it: no hybrid can cross the ring of stones, and one who reaches past a stone pulls back as if from a stove. So they want the ward broken. That isn't malice: they see the fungus as the valley's next season and the ring as a jar with them in it, and they have kin on the other side. They call Wardens stone-cutters and the holdfast's people wax-women, for the smoke. They're the descendants' cousins, which neither side knew until Tam Reedsdaughter carried a verse of her grandmother's song to Gill. One of them, Hollow, listens to the whole of the ground from the Threadwell, behind the Threaded Wall, and claims to speak for the network itself; Hollow admits to no longer knowing where the ground's wants end and Hollow's begin. Hollow makes the offer: open the first line at the Keystone and the hybrids walk out, and the ground with them. Gill was the child who held on to the Sixth Stone sixty years ago while a young Warden re-cut it, and still remembers that he didn't look up.
goals: Break the ward and let the network grow
Be recognised as a people, not a plague, and walk their kin home past the stones
Teach sporecraft to outsiders who will listen
members: Those who listen to the network

regions.name: The Landing
regions.description: Open meadow at the valley mouth on the southern edge, where the company's boats tied up and the camp stands. A stream runs through grass, gorse and flax, with fallen wood along the tree line and stone underfoot. Chickens gone feral and rabbits are the only things to fight, and adders in the long grass. This is tier 0: flint tools, wooden clubs, slings and linen. Camp has the workbench, the campfire, the contract board and Ansel Morrow's table at its northern edge.
regions.lore: The Landing was never hidden. It lay outside the ward, and its people were moved downriver before the ward went up, so it holds only traces: the stones of field walls in the grass, a forged hinge, a lane that runs north into the trees and stops. The feral chickens are descended from the farms' flocks. Nothing here is colonised. The first hint of the fungus is Ada Thwaite's observation that the mushrooms past the tree line grow in rows.
regions.climate: mild and open, with river mist in the mornings
resources: Wild herbs at the meadow's edge

regions.name: Southwood
regions.description: Birch and oak forest wrapping the Landing on three sides: the first real wilderness. Wolves, boar and crow swarms live here, and a hunter's lodge stands in a clearing. Timber, herbs, bone, hide and ordinary mushrooms make tier-1 gear: bone-and-hardwood tools, spears, shortbows, hide and leather, and the first torch.
regions.lore: The Southwood grew over farmland in the 120 years the valley was closed, so walls, wells and cellars lie under the leaf litter. It lay south of the wardstones, and its families were taken downriver before the ward went up: a list of them is scratched in the cellar of the Sunken Farm, beside a cracked Warden boundary stone. Jory Flint, the company's hunter, works out of a lodge built from a fallen farmhouse's beams. At the Far Stile on the northern edge, a dead hind grown over with white in rows is the first colonised animal anyone has seen.

regions.name: The Scarp
regions.description: Hill pasture, scree, crags and an old quarry along the west flank, reached from the western Southwood. Tier 2 for mining and smithing: copper and tin outcrops a bone pick can scratch, soapstone for moulds, cliff yews that need a bronze axe, and rock crabs, cave bats and mine stalkers. Bett Oakes, the company smith, runs a forge in the ore-house of an old mine, where charcoal from Southwood oak turns copper and tin to bronze. The galleries behind the forge are dark and need a light, and hold the rich seams and the wardstone seam. Below them the Wardens walled up a level that has since been unsealed: an iron seam a bronze pick can just bite, in the dark. Iron wants twice bronze's charcoal at the forge.
regions.lore: The mine was dug by the Wardens, and not for ore. Its adits are cut dead square with warding lines over every doorway, and the deepest gallery ends at a seam of grey-green wardstone cut back in twelve numbered blocks: the ring of wardstones across the valley was quarried here and hauled north. Beside the twelfth gap is cut THE RING IS RAISED. SEAL THE LEVEL, and the level was never sealed. The Tally Cairn on the Scarp's high end carries twelve strokes. Bett Oakes has worked most of this out from the tool marks alone. Warding staves and focus-stones are cut from the wardstone seam, and it's the obvious place to mend the ring from. The rock crabs' shells turn blade and arrow alike, a hint that another kind of force is needed. Below the wardstone the Wardens walled the next level shut with a warding line cut across the wall like a bar across a door; its mortar has crumbled, and the rust-red iron seam beyond is the valley's tier-3 metal.
regions.climate: dry, windy uplands; cold and dark underground
inhabitants: Cave bats, rock crabs and mine stalkers
Bett Oakes, the company smith, at the mine forge
resources: Iron from the unsealed level below the wardstone, with a light and a bronze pick

regions.name: The Sinks
regions.description: Fen, reedbeds, clay banks and a wide cold mere across the east flank, reached from the eastern Southwood. Tier 2 for fishing, pottery and leather: bog moss, reeds cut with a sickle, peat and clay dug with a turf spade, sand off the lake shore, perch from withy traps and glass-floated nets. The wading ground is cold enough to slow anyone's hands, and waders or a hot fen broth only soften it. Col Reeve, the company's potter, keeps a turf kiln on a rise above the fen that fires jars and melts the valley's only glass, with peat-water tanning pits beside it where gut bowstrings, yew longbows, mossback waders and moss spore-wraps are made. Pike lie in the channels, mossback toads spit from the hummocks, and at Heron Carr in the north the first colonised creature stands among the roots. An old causeway of fitted stone crosses the fen to a Warden boundary stone.
regions.lore: The Sinks were fished and cut for peat long before the ward: the cuttings are stepped and the weir stakes in the mere are older than the company's charter. The Sinks lie outside the ring of wardstones, but the network runs under the fen closer to the surface than anywhere else outside it, and the soft ground rises and falls at night over its threads. Col Reeve calls it breathing. At Heron Carr the network has taken the herons, the first creatures players find grown over outside the ring. The boundary stone at the end of the Old Causeway is a lesser Warden stone like the Sunken Farm's lintel. Its lines are cracked on the fen side and the threads have grown into the grooves, following the lines as if learning them. Peat water tans hide dark and tight and preserves what falls into it. The Sinks supply the strings, waders and glass the Scarp's bronze can't do without, and the heron's pale growth is what a Warden sets a first staff against.
regions.climate: cold, wet fen and still water
inhabitants: Pike, mossback toads and colonised herons
Col Reeve, the company potter and fisher, at the kiln
resources: Pale growth from the colonised herons

regions.name: The Wardline
regions.description: The middle band of the valley, north of the Southwood's Far Stile: walled fields gone feral, sunken lanes tunnelled by hedges, roofless steadings with bees in the walls, and hedgerows with white threads running under the branches. The twelve wardstones ring the Bloom; the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh and Eighth stand along the Wardline's northern edge where it meets the Bloom, with a straight ward ditch cut between them. Tier 3 and contested. The air carries spores everywhere, so a mask becomes necessary: the Sinks' moss spore-wrap takes a little off, the holdfast's waxed mask and tinctures a good deal more, and nothing takes all of it. Feral hound packs run the lanes, mossback wolves hunt the hedges, and host wanderers stand in the long grass facing the stones. The descendants' holdfast sits in the middle of it behind its own walls, with Old Wick at the gate, Tam Reedsdaughter's loom and apothecary at the back, a contract board by the gate, and smudge fires of mugwort that keep the air inside clearer. Square Warden houses by the stones still hold salvageable Warden steel for anyone with an iron pick.
regions.lore: The ward was raised by the twelve stones of the ring, but it reached out as far as the lesser boundary stones in the Southwood and the Sinks. Everyone south of the boundary stones was carted downriver first. The families between the boundary stones and the ring, the Wickens, Reeds, Dunnings, Hales, Thackerys and thirty more, were told they would be fetched within the week, and then the stones were lit around them. A roll in the Warden's house by the Fifth Stone lists them unmarked, with a note at the foot: 'Sister E. asks again that these be told. Refused.' Each stone had a sworn keeper and a square Warden house barred from outside. Sister Edith stayed at the Seventh Stone; her journal is under the hearthstone of her hut. It records that she went to the Reeds and the Wickens herself, and that on the night the stones were lit the Reeds' daughter came to the line and called her name, and Edith didn't answer. The survivors walled themselves into the holdfast. Their names have worn down (Wicken to Wick), but they still match the Wardens' roll. The hosts in the long grass are the ones who gave themselves to the network in the first years, kept as they were by the ground; they drift to the stones and stand facing north, as if waiting to be let back in.
regions.climate: temperate and overgrown, with a faint haze of spores over the grass on still days
inhabitants: The descendants of the holdfast: Old Wick, Tam Reedsdaughter, Nell-of-the-Ditch and some sixty more
Host wanderers, feral hound packs and mossback wolves
Sister Edith, dead, present only in her journal at the Seventh Stone
resources: Salvaged Warden steel from the Warden houses by the stones
Feral wool snagged on the lane hedges, and flax and wheat gone wild in the walled fields
Beeswax and honey from wild hives in the steading walls
Mugwort from the hedges and ditches, and comfrey from the old kitchen gardens
Grey threads from fallen hosts, and pale growth from mossback wolves

regions.name: The Bloom
regions.description: Old forest inside the wardstone ring, north of the Wardline, gone under the growth: trunks sheathed in pale threads, colonised birch stands weeping amber resin, puffball glades where every step raises a cloud, stony hollows crusted over in horn-hard chitin, elk wallows under threaded oaks, and the grown-over cottages of the old valley with hosts standing in the doorways. Tier 4. The spores are twice the Wardline's, and worse in the puffball glades: a waxed mask only halves them, and the holdfast's Filter Respirator, with spore-glass eyes, does better without ever stopping them. Hosts swing hard, host-clusters burst in clouds of spores that go through mail, colonised elk take a lot of killing, and spore-moth swarms settle on anything warm. Fungal materials are dangerous to gather and valuable: mycelium mats and spore resin need an iron axe, chitin an iron pick, and the threaded oaks and crusted boulders chitin-edged tools. They make mycelium leather, chitin armour, the chitin blade and the spine-bow. The old village green, the Standing Green, has a ring of hosts round its well. North-east of it Gill keeps the growing pit, terraced beds laid out the way the Reeds lay a kitchen garden, where sporecraft is taught to anyone Gill trusts with a chitin dibber: the Sporecraft Wand and Thread Balm are grown there. North of the pit the forest ends at the Threaded Wall, a barn-high wall of warm grey threads round the Heart. The only way through is where it hangs loose like a curtain, straight north of the pit, and parts if you push.
regions.lore: This was the heart of the old valley's settlement before it was sealed, and the ring was drawn round the worst of the growth, not in front of it. The twelve stones run round the Bloom: the Fifth to the Eighth along the Wardline's edge, the Fourth and the rest of the low numbers up the Bloom's eastern side against the Sinks, the Ninth to the Twelfth up its western side under the Scarp. Nobody has stood at the Fourth since the lighting, and its lines have been filled with growth laid in groove by groove, which hosts can't do. It's where the turned became hosts and where their children, the hybrids, were born into the network. The hosts of the Standing Green grew together where they stood round the well; the hybrids call them the parents. Gill, the first hybrid to talk to outsiders, keeps the growing pit and is Tam Reedsdaughter's cousin without either of them knowing it: Gill's father was Davy Reed, who walked into the wood laughing the spring after the stones were lit. Gill never knew Davy as a man, only as a song the ground sings; the second verse, 'and the ground came up to meet him, and it's holding him yet', is the one the holdfast won't sing. Tam and Gill have met at the pit, and Tam has been over the ring. The hybrids can't cross the stones, so Gill walked her only as far as the Sixth.
regions.climate: close, humid and thick with spores
inhabitants: Gill and the other hybrids, at the growing pit
Hollow, behind the Threaded Wall at the Threadwell
resources: Mycelium mats from grown-through logs and spore resin from weeping birches (iron axe)
Fungal chitin from the crust on stones and stumps (iron pick), and more from crusted boulders (chitin-edged pick)
Threaded heartwood from threaded oaks (chitin-edged axe)
Threaded spines and elk hide from colonised elk, moth down from spore-moths, grey threads from hosts
Spore-glass, fused at the Sinks kiln from glass and spore resin

regions.name: The Heart
regions.description: A small hollow at the north-centre of the valley, ringed all round by the Threaded Wall, where the network comes up out of the ground. Tier 5 and the endgame. The only way in is the Parting, where the wall hangs loose north of the growing pit. Inside is bare warm mat, hanging curtains of thread and ridges of heartshell, and nothing to gather at all. The spores are twice the Bloom's and thickest at the Threadwell, where the network swells up like water over a spring: even a Warden's Respirator and a tincture leave you bleeding. The Grown walk here, bodies the Heart grew for itself rather than took: Threshers with flails of shell, Slingers that whip barbs from a sinew arm, and Singers that hum the Heart's note until the air presses on you. At the Keepers' Camp the Heart-Warden still keeps watch. Everything tier 5 is made from what they drop: heartshell at the forge, grown sinew at the tanning rack, humming thread in the growing pit's beds, and the Warden's Respirator, re-cut at the warding table from the one the Heart-Warden wears. Here the question of repairing or breaking the ward is finally put, at the Keystone by the Threadwell: re-cut with the Warden's stylus, or unpicked with the chitin dibber.
regions.lore: Nobody knows what the Heart is: the network's oldest part, or its mind, or only the place it happened to start. The Threaded Wall has grown round it since the sealing, and it's still growing; the hybrids say it parts for whoever the ground has decided to let in. The ring was keyed from here. The Keepers walked in wearing the order's own respirators, bronze and horn with warded filters, camped by the Threadwell, and cut the first line into a slab of wardstone at its lip: the Keystone, one long closed line with twelve spurs, one for each stone. Every stone answers to it, so the ward can only be mended or broken at the Keystone, and its lines are still clean. A closed line has to be closed from inside, so the first line closes on whoever cuts it. One of them never came out: Keeper Joss Wicken, a valley boy who went south to the order young, whose brother's family farmed north of the stones. He keyed the ring with his own kin inside it, sent the other Keepers out, and stayed. The order wrote him down as dead at the sealing. He is the Heart-Warden, a Keeper's knot on his shoulder and his name scratched in his respirator's cheek-guard, still keeping watch at the Keepers' Camp, grown through at every joint. The Grown aren't hosts: there's nobody inside them, only shapes the network remembers. Hollow sits at the Threadwell with legs gone down into the swell, hears the whole of the ground, and speaks for the network, or claims to. At the Keystone a warder's stylus can re-cut the first line clean, around wardstone and a thread of the Heart, and the ring holds for another hundred years; a sporecrafter's dibber can open its spurs from the inside, the way something grows, and every stone goes quiet at once. Ansel asks for the first, Hollow for the second, and each player chooses once and for good. Re-cutting keeps the Bloom and its spores off the holdfast and the settlement and keeps the hybrids in the jar; opening it lets Gill walk Tam home past the stones, and lets the Bloom walk down the valley behind them. The bible doesn't say which the valley got. Whatever players decide here, someone pays for it.
regions.climate: warm, still and thick with spores
inhabitants: The Grown: Threshers, Slingers and Singers
The Heart-Warden, at the Keepers' Camp
resources: Heartshell from Threshers, and some from Slingers and the Heart-Warden
A cracked Warden's respirator and Warden steel from the Heart-Warden

history.name: The Valley Settled
history.description: Long before the ward, the valley was ordinary farmland and forest with a few villages and a road downriver. Its people farmed the Landing and the middle valley, mined the Scarp, fished the Sinks and paid a small tithe to the Crown. The Wardens were a local order of stoneworkers and keepers who knew how to draw on the bedrock, and they kept the old stones and settled disputes.
history.significance: The field walls, lanes and cellars players find are this valley's remains. Descendant family names come from these villages.

history.name: The First Growth
history.description: About 125 years ago the fungus surfaced in the upper valley. First came strange crops of mushrooms in rows, then colonised livestock, then people who walked into the woods and stood still. Nobody knows where it came from. The Wardens found it ran through the ground under the whole upper valley as one living network.
history.significance: The fungus the settlers meet is the same network, 125 years older and much bigger.

history.name: The Raising of the Ward
history.description: About 120 years ago the Wardens raised a ring of twelve wardstones across the middle of the valley and bound them into a ward that held the network in. The ward reached out as far as the lesser boundary stones in the Southwood and the Sinks. The Wardens moved everyone south of the boundary stones downriver first. The families between the boundary stones and the ring were told they would be fetched within the week, and they weren't: the Keepers judged that the growth was already in their fields and that they would carry it south. A roll of their names hangs in the Warden house by the Fifth Stone, unmarked. Each wardstone was kept by a sworn Warden, and some stayed at their stones for good. Sister Edith of the Seventh Stone had begged the Keepers to warn them and was refused; she went to the Reeds and the Wickens herself, then stayed at her stone and kept a watch until she died. The ring was keyed from the Heart, where the four Keepers cut the first line into the Keystone. A closed line closes on whoever cuts it, so Keeper Joss Wicken, whose brother's family were on the roll, sent the others out and stayed inside to close it; the order wrote him down as dead at the sealing. The order was sworn to silence.
history.significance: This is the Wardens' secret and the root of the descendants' grievance. The wardstone ring still stands along the Wardline's northern edge, Edith's journal is still under her hearth, and Ansel Morrow knows what's in it.

history.name: The Abandoned Divide
history.description: Inside the ward, the abandoned families had to live beside the fungus. Some walled themselves into a holdfast in the middle band and learned masks, mugwort, remedies and patience. They became the descendants. Others gave themselves to the network to survive and became its hosts; the ground has kept them as they were, and they still wander the long grass and stand at the stones. Davy Reed, Tam Reedsdaughter's grandmother's brother, walked into the wood laughing the spring after the stones were lit. The children of hosts like him were born inside the network, thinking and feeling and at peace with it. They became the hybrids.
history.significance: The descendants and the hybrids are cousins who took different roads. Gill is Davy Reed's child, which makes Tam Reedsdaughter and Gill cousins; neither knows it yet. Tam sings her grandmother's song about Davy over the still.

history.name: The Order Fades
history.description: Downriver, the Crown marked the valley impassable and forgot it. With nothing to keep, the Wardens dwindled to a few old members, the craft half-lost and the oath kept. Sixty years ago, with six of them left, the order sent its youngest, Ansel Morrow, nineteen, up the valley alone to re-cut the Sixth Stone where it was failing. He was told nobody was alive inside. His mark, A.M. RE-CUT, is under the moss on the stone's south face, and on its inner face a child's hand scraped the growth away. The child was Gill, Davy Reed's child, reaching for the side of the stone its father came from. Ansel finished the line anyway, and the stone burned the child's hand off it. He kept that to himself for sixty years.
history.significance: Only a few Wardens, like Ansel Morrow, are left who know the truth or the craft, and Ansel carried a part of his own until he confessed it at Wick's gate.

history.name: The Reopening
history.description: This spring the weather over the valley broke and the old roads opened. The charter company got a licence from the Crown and landed settlers at the valley mouth. As far as the company knows, the valley is empty land. Ansel Morrow came upriver at his own expense.
history.significance: This is the start of play. The ward is failing, and the settlers are walking toward what it held.

history.name: The Reckoning at the Gate
history.description: In the settlers' first year a Warden stood at the holdfast's gate and said it all. Ansel Morrow, the last sworn, brought Sister Edith's book from under her hearthstone at the Seventh Stone, with the upper families written out again on its last page and under them I will tell them myself. In front of Old Wick he said that the order took the southern families down and told the rest to stay put knowing it wasn't coming back; that he had re-cut the Sixth Stone at nineteen while Davy Reed's child held on to it from inside; and that the Heart-Warden is Joss Wicken, Wick's grandmother's uncle, who keyed the first line and stayed. Wick said it wasn't forgiven, but it was said. Then he sent the Warden up to the Sixth Stone to say it again to Gill across the line, and Ansel looked up. Meanwhile Hollow, at the Threadwell, put the network's offer to the same settler: open the first line.
history.significance: The Wardens' confession and the descendants' reckoning are done, and nobody left is keeping the secret. What remains is the choice at the Keystone, which Wick refuses to make, Ansel says isn't his, and Hollow can't make for itself.

history.name: The First Line
history.description: Whoever reaches the Keystone with both crafts in hand decides, once, what happens to the ring. Re-cut with a stylus around wardstone and a thread of the Heart, the first line closes and every stone goes hot at once, like a hand closing; the ground goes quiet for the first time in living memory, the Bloom stays behind the stones, and Gill and Hollow and every hybrid stay with it for another hundred years. Ansel makes his last focus from a chip of the Keystone, and Tam carries bread up to the Sixth Stone at dusk for a cousin who can't come down. Unpicked with a dibber, the spurs open and every stone goes cold and quiet; the Keeper at the Keepers' Camp is let rest, Gill walks Tam home through the holdfast's gate and sees a sheep, and the Bloom follows a field at a time, the ward ditch white by morning and smudge fires and masks only slowing it. Hollow grows a wand from a seed of the well for whoever opened it. Each settler who stands there makes this choice for themselves; the valley's history doesn't record one answer.
history.significance: This is the endgame. Neither ending is canon: content written after it must work whichever way a player chose, and never assume the ring is standing or fallen.

characterPatterns: Settlers: ordinary, slightly rustic English given name and surname (e.g., Hobb Carrow, Maren Pike, Ada Thwaite)
Wardens: the same stock, formal, with a title or a stone (e.g., Warden-Keeper Ansel Morrow, Sister Edith of the Seventh Stone)
Descendants: settler names worn down over 120 years, plus a byname (e.g., Tam Reedsdaughter, Old Wick, Nell-of-the-Ditch)
Hybrids: a single name from the forest floor, a texture or kind of growth (e.g., Lichen, Gill, Softwater, the one called Hollow)
Company officials: surname and office (e.g., Quartermaster Pike, Clerk Hatherley)
placePatterns: Plain English compounds named for what's there (e.g., Flint Beck, Tanner's Cut)
Named for what happened there (e.g., Gallows Oak, Hollow Stair)
A person's name and a feature (e.g., Carrow's Bench, Reeve's Kiln)
Wardstones are numbered (e.g., the Seventh Stone, the First Stone)
Never fantasy jargon; the outside world is only 'the Crown' or 'downriver'
itemPatterns: Material + object (e.g., Bronze Sickle, Flint Axe, Linen Shirt)
A treatment + object (e.g., Waxed Mask, Tanned Jerkin)
Owner or maker + object for special gear (e.g., Warden's Respirator)
Food as it'd be said at a campfire (e.g., Rabbit Stew, Nettle Tea)
No glowing, ancient or legendary adjectives
